title: Loss functions: why fitting is really optimising
intro: Fitting = minimizing a loss. Once you see this perspective, you recognize the common thread across all models.
keyPoints: A loss is a penalty score: how wrong is this one prediction?
Squared loss (quadratic error) is the default for regression.
0-1 loss counts mistakes but is not smooth → impossible to optimise nicely.

blocks.html: A loss function is a penalty score for how poorly the model does on the training data; fitting = shifting coefficients until that score is minimal. Note the distinction: loss is for fitting, score for judging.

blocks.label: squared loss (linear regression)
blocks.caption: Least squares: the sum of squared errors over all training examples.

rows: "which parameters make the error on the training data small?"
"how well does the model perform on (new) data?"

blocks.html: For classification you count mistakes: the 0-1 loss is 0 (correct) or 1 (wrong) per example; the sum is exactly the number of errors. Conceptually clean, but not differentiable and therefore hard to minimize directly — LR and SVMs use a smooth approximation.

blocks.label: 0-1 loss
blocks.caption: The sum over all training examples = the number of mistakes on the training set.

blocks.html: With scipy.optimize.minimize you can minimize any function. Numerical optimization rarely gives exact zeros but values very close (e.g. 10−8) — which is perfectly fine.

blocks.caption: scipy.optimize.minimize in action
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# Minimise y = x^2, starting from x = 3
result = minimize(np.square, x0=3.0)
print('minimum at x =', result.x[0])
print('loss value    =', result.fun)

# And from a different starting point
result2 = minimize(np.square, x0=-10.0)
print('from -10      :', result2.x[0])

blocks.html: Don't expect exact zeros: numerical optimisation gives answers "in the neighbourhood" — \( \approx 10^{-8} \) is a perfectly fine result.
